newsitem.title: USA: US YIELD CURVE - Big flattening points to rate hike.
newsitem.headline: US YIELD CURVE - Big flattening points to rate hike.

text.p: It took some time, but the U.S. Treasury yield curve finally flattened on Thursday, a sign that more market partipants are convinced Federal Reserve policy makers will raise rates at next Tuesday's meeting.

Months after the market began talking about a possible Fed tightening and hours after some highly hawkish comments from Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan, the spread between the two-year note and the 30-year bond narrowed to roughly 71 basis points from 77 at Wednesday's close.
The last time the spread was so narrow was in late February, after the first leg of Greenspan's Humphrey Hawkins testimony.

"It's logical curve behavior," said Patrick Dimick, chief U.S. Treasury market strategist at UBS Securities LLC. "We had a strong Philadelphia Fed report along with Greenspan reiterating his very hawkish stance from Humphrey Hawkins. That combination led to a dramatic curve flattening and a resurgence at the long end."

The two-year note's yield rose to 6.25 percent from 6.22 percent, while the bond's yield fell to 6.96 percent from 6.99 percent. That, players said, is an indication that the short end expects a tightening, while the long end is confident the Fed remains vigilant on inflation.

One senior trader at a primary dealership said that dealers put on flattening trades, selling the short end in the morning and buying the long end in the afternoon -- the main reason why it took so long during the day for the curve to actually flatten.
He noted that dealers added to existing curve flattening trades as well as setting up new ones.

Greenspan, in testimony before Congress's Joint Economic Committee, gave an upbeat assessment of the U.S. economy, stressing strong economic growth, rising wages and consumers who continue to spend, albeit without concrete signs of inflation.
Still, to head off future inflation, Greenspan said it is important to act "promptly -- ideally pre-emptively."
"Greenspan told you today that he was going to tighten," said Mark Mahoney, Treasury market strategist at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp.

"All that's left is the debate on Tuesday," Dimick added. "He tried to soften up the market, and indeed succeeded because with the short-end moving back to 6.25 percent on two-years, the market is finally taking the Fed's (tightening) threats seriously."
Dimick said there was "no bid for two-year paper" or bills for that matter after Greenspan's speech.

Talk in the market of a near-term tightening has been off and on since July. But even after last month's Humphrey Hawkins testimony, and a string of strong economic data, the market was not fully convinced the Fed was ready to pull the trigger.

A Reuters poll taken last week found just 17 of 44 Wall Street economists -- 39 percent -- forecasting a rate hike on March 25. But a subsequent survey released Thursday showed 34 of 48 economists -- 71 percent -- predicting a rate hike next week.
"We are fully priced for a 25 basis point tightening," Mahoney said.
He noted that the curve could flatten further the next few sessions as dealers set up shorts ahead of the two-year note auction on Tuesday and as buyers emerge when the bond hits 7.0 percent.
